Patient fall detection alarm

CSULB, fall 2026, team of 3

A bedside device that alerts a caregiver the moment a patient falls.

The problem

Caregivers cannot watch every patient at every moment, and a fall that goes unnoticed can turn serious.

What I built

An Arduino-based device with a tilt sensor, LCD, piezo buzzer, and LED, which I designed, programmed, and tested with two teammates.

The result

A working prototype that sounds an alarm, flashes the LED, and shows a message as soon as a fall is detected. We documented it in a progress report and presented it in lab.

Next version

Swap the tilt sensor for an accelerometer and compare the two by accuracy and false alarms.

  • Arduino
  • C++
  • Sensors
  • Embedded systems
  • Patient safety

How it works

The device runs on an Arduino Mega and watches a tilt ball switch wired to pin D7. While the patient is upright, the switch stays in its normal state and the 16×2 LCD reads “Patient is upright.” When the patient falls, the ball inside the switch shifts and the switch changes state. The Arduino detects the change, switches the LCD to “Patient fell,” sounds the piezo buzzer on D8 as a siren, and flashes an LED on D9 through a 220 Ω resistor. A 10 kΩ alarm potentiometer on analog pin A0 lets a caregiver enable or disable the buzzer, and a second potentiometer sets the LCD contrast. The LCD runs in 4-bit mode, so only four data lines (D2 to D5) plus RS and E are needed, which keeps the wiring simple.

Robotic Arm Design & Prototyping

Orange Coast College · ENGR A110 · Fall 2023 · Team project of five

A low-cost, manually operated robotic arm built from cardboard, wooden craft sticks, twine, rubber bands, and tape.

Project overview

I worked with a team of four other engineering students to design and build a low-cost, manually operated robotic arm using limited materials and strict size limits. The goal was a functional arm that could safely lift, hold, and release a full water bottle, which meant applying core mechanical engineering principles under real constraints.

Design objectives

  • Lift: raise a full water bottle at least 15 cm above desk level.
  • Hold: keep the bottle at that height for 10 seconds.
  • Release: lower and release the bottle without tipping it over.

All three had to be met within the material and size limits.

Engineering design and development

  • Conceptual design: developed preliminary sketches to set the arm’s geometry, reach, joints, and gripping mechanism.
  • Structural engineering: added triangular cardboard trusses and wooden reinforcements to improve rigidity and load-bearing capability.
  • Mechanical analysis: applied statics, torque, leverage, and force distribution to guide structural decisions.
  • Prototype fabrication: built the arm from inexpensive materials, including cardboard, wooden craft sticks, twine, rubber bands, and tape.
  • Design optimization: evaluated structural weaknesses and explored changes to improve stability, strength, and controlled movement.
  • Mechanical design
  • Rapid prototyping
  • Structural reinforcement
  • Statics & torque analysis
  • Design constraints
  • Problem-solving
  • Team collaboration

Project takeaways

This project gave me hands-on experience turning engineering concepts into a physical prototype under real-world constraints. It strengthened my understanding of mechanical structures, material limits, load distribution, and the iterative design process.

It also showed me how to balance function, structural integrity, cost, and manufacturability when developing robotic systems.
